scope: Manual case study prompted by letter 301. Three incoming letters linked to two outgoing letters; not a corpus-wide receipt or reply audit.

matches.match_basis: Darwin identifies Catherine and January 1836; the surviving 29 January letter mentions printed extracts, Erasmus furnishing his house, and the expected Parker child, all taken up in the reply. Earliest inferred receipt is 1 June from his arrival two days before the reply.

receipt.known_by_basis: Explicit acknowledgment in DCP-LETT-302; this is an upper bound, not the delivery day.

matches.match_basis: Darwin explicitly identifies Catherine's October letter. The surviving 30 October 1835 letter agrees in sender and month; the year follows the sequence and the comparison with the later January letter received at the Cape.

receipt.known_by_basis: Explicit acknowledgment in DCP-LETT-306; this is an upper bound, not the delivery day.

matches.match_basis: Darwin explicitly identifies Susan's November letter and responds to the reported praise of his collections by Sedgwick, which appears in the surviving 22 November 1835 letter.

receipt.known_by_basis: Explicit acknowledgment in DCP-LETT-306; this is an upper bound, not the delivery day.

observations.scope: Correspondence and news from home; do not generalize mechanically to every correspondent.
observations.evidence_anchor: the date of the last letter I received was 13 months ago
observations.interpretation: The newest letter he mentions was itself dated about thirteen months earlier. This does not date its arrival or prove that no local letters reached him. Preserve the approximation; do not turn it into a precise global exclusion cutoff.

observations.scope: Catherine's January letter received; older home correspondence still missing.
observations.evidence_anchor: Nine months’ letters are wandering over the wide ocean
observations.interpretation: Receipt of a newer letter does not establish receipt of all earlier letters. His expectation that the missing letters would arrive only after England is a contemporary prediction, not an actual receipt date.

observations.evidence_anchor: I daresay, amongst them there was a letter from you
observations.interpretation: The missing-mail report extends beyond family correspondence, but a specific Henslow letter in the missing batch is conjectural.

observations.scope: A mail bundle reported at dispatch.
observations.evidence_anchor: There are letters, but the bundle has not been opened.
observations.interpretation: Do not make the unseen bundle's contents available to this response. The flap note is undated; the bundle contents are not enumerated.

observations.scope: Catherine October 1835 and Susan November 1835 letters.
observations.evidence_anchor: At Ascension I received Catherines letter of October & yours of November
observations.interpretation: Both are known by this reply; exact receipt dates at Ascension remain unresolved. The location and sequence place the receipt in July, but no precise July day is assigned.

training_implications: Keep composition date and availability evidence separate; never replace an original date.
Use the identified incoming letter or letters as actual correspondence context for the attested reply.
For general memory retrieval, the conservative activation date is a known-by upper bound. Same-day order still needs evidence; the named reply is explicitly supported.
Do not infer that all earlier letters became available when a newer letter arrived.
Delivery at a port and reading a bundle are separate events.
The quoted report of Sedgwick in Susan's letter is information conveyed to Darwin through an included incoming letter; no separate third-party letter has been added.
Preserve unpaired Darwin letters as dated grounding, without inventing missing inbound prompts.
